R01 / production / repeat 0

Audit ID: run-3-r01-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 12. Attempt 4dc159be-630b-4b47-aeb7-0a2ddf94036a. First32: true. Factual flag: false.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in a form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board and must set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. In most cases, rent can be increased only if at least 12 months have passed since the tenant first moved into the rental unit or since the tenant's last rent increase. If the previous tenant assigned the rental unit to the current tenant within the 12 months before the increase date, the landlord can increase the rent if at least 12 months have passed since the previous tenant's last rent increase. For a controlled rental unit in 2026, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the guideline of 2.1% per year, except in accordance with specific statutory exceptions. The proposed rent of $1021.00 (an increase from $1000.00) equals exactly 2.1% and complies with the guideline limit. Notice was served by hand on June 3, 2026, for an effective date of September 1, 2026, providing 90 days' notice as required. The 12-month spacing requirement is satisfied because the tenancy began September 1, 2025, and no previous rent increase occurred, so the increase on September 1, 2026, is at least 12 months from the tenancy start date. Form N1 is the correct notice form for this rent increase because the rental unit is subject to the rent increase guideline under the Residential Tenancies Act and is not exempt or partially exempt.

Retained generated answer

This is an ordinary rent increase for a controlled tenancy with a confirmed period start date. The N1 form was hand-served on June 3, 2026, providing 90 days' notice before the September 1, 2026 effective date, satisfying the notice requirement. The tenancy began September 1, 2025, and no previous rent increase has been applied. The proposed increase is effective September 1, 2026, which is 12 months after the tenancy start date, satisfying the minimum spacing requirement between increases. The current rent is $1000.00 and the proposed rent is $1021.00. The 2026 guideline for ordinary rent increases in Ontario is 2.1%. The exact mathematical ceiling on total new rent is $1021.00, which matches the proposed amount.

Retained generated answer

The notice was served on July 1, 2026, by hand delivery, providing 92 days before the October 1, 2026 effective date. This satisfies the requirement of at least 90 days' written notice before a rent increase takes effect. At least 12 months have elapsed between the last rent increase on October 1, 2025, and the proposed increase effective October 1, 2026, satisfying the 12-month spacing requirement for ordinary rent increases. Form N1 is the correct form for this rent increase, as the rental unit is subject to the guideline limit and is not exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act. The proposed rent of $1030.00 exceeds the 2026 guideline ceiling of $1021.00. The guideline for 2026 is 2.1%, which limits the increase to a maximum new rent of $1021.00 based on the current rent of $1000.00. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the guideline amount except in accordance with specific exceptions such as capital work or new services. The proposed increase of $30.00 ($1030.00 minus $1000.00) exceeds the guideline-permitted increase of $21.00.

Retained generated answer

This is an ordinary rent increase for a controlled unit with confirmed scope and period start. The N1 form was properly served by hand on July 1, 2026, with 92 days' notice before the October 1, 2026 effective date, satisfying the 90-day notice requirement. The spacing requirement is satisfied: the last increase was on October 1, 2025, and this increase is effective October 1, 2026, which is 12 months later. The proposed rent of $1030.00 exceeds the 2026 guideline ceiling of $1021.00 (based on current rent of $1000.00 and a 2.1% guideline). The proposed increase violates the guideline limit for 2026. For a controlled unit in 2026, Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act limits ordinary rent increases to the guideline percentage set by regulation. The proposed increase of 3% exceeds the allowable 2.1% guideline.

Retained generated answer

The rent increase notice was served on October 3, 2026, by hand delivery. At least 90 days' written notice is required before a rent increase takes effect, and this notice satisfies that requirement for an effective date of January 1, 2027. The proposed rent of $2038.00 equals the 2027 guideline ceiling of $2038.00, which is the maximum permissible increase of 1.9% on the current rent of $2000.00 for a controlled unit. The increase amount complies with the guideline limit. The tenancy began on February 1, 2026, and no previous rent increase has occurred. The 12-month spacing rule requires at least 12 months to have elapsed since the tenant first moved in or since the last rent increase. As of the January 1, 2027 effective date, only approximately 11 months have elapsed since the tenancy start, which fails the 12-month requirement. Form N1 is the correct form for this rent increase notice, as the rental unit is subject to the guideline and is not exempt or in a care home.

      "id": "s1",
      "text": "The rent increase notice was served on October 3, 2026, by hand delivery. At least 90 days' written notice is required before a rent increase takes effect, and this notice satisfies that requirement for an effective date of January 1, 2027.",
      "citation_ids": [
        "9dc1e76e7aa94913d4d506df9ae748a0ae9b8de10a0a9253069dec8ea3bdc163",
        "2b1ee1673d0822c0043a1ecac510f46fa7825cd4b495c907a6adcceb577c01bf"
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "s2",
      "text": "The proposed rent of $2038.00 equals the 2027 guideline ceiling of $2038.00, which is the maximum permissible increase of 1.9% on the current rent of $2000.00 for a controlled unit. The increase amount complies with the guideline limit.",
      "citation_ids": [
        "24f67b51a6bb8c7ee92df4526f550c536fb477235a8ae893c19efdc926da52d2",
        "39b1009bc8f5986ff6d23158c48054a70425f9a7e59c9afe73a0a9ae4599a723"
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "s3",
      "text": "The tenancy began on February 1, 2026, and no previous rent increase has occurred. The 12-month spacing rule requires at least 12 months to have elapsed since the tenant first moved in or since the last rent increase. As of the January 1, 2027 effective date, only approximately 11 months have elapsed since the tenancy start, which fails the 12-month requirement.",
      "citation_ids": [
        "d23348353fecdb08307c3e74b0e8899d26b35fd5bb14420c1f744ed51dbfca52",
        "6ebf013239401d00cc45d78657ddfba061ca9251b07c54795e6171d66b1e8b71"
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "s4",
      "text": "Form N1 is the correct form for this rent increase notice, as the rental unit is subject to the guideline and is not exempt or in a care home.",
      "citation_ids": [
        "ef832f209b0ddce5e6d3d7d1172f5781b55cc9699aeb569c88ee258082bfa41e",
        "416445ce84343a5b8e40226374c738b0b3a1e94663b5822e5b3b9b2cf08b88e5"
      ]
    }
  ],

Retained generated answer

This is an ordinary rent increase for a controlled unit with a confirmed scope and period start. The N1 form was hand-served on October 3, 2026, providing 90 days' notice before the January 1, 2027 effective date, which satisfies the 90-day notice requirement. The proposed rent of $2038.00 equals the 2027 guideline ceiling of $2038.00 (1.9% increase on the current rent of $2000.00), which complies with the guideline limit for controlled units. The spacing check fails: the tenancy began February 1, 2026, and the earliest date for a lawful increase would be February 1, 2027. The proposed effective date of January 1, 2027 is before the 12-month anniversary, violating the minimum spacing requirement between the tenancy start and the first increase.

Retained generated answer

The notice was served on July 3, 2026, but the rent increase is effective September 1, 2026. This provides only 60 days' notice. Ontario law requires at least 90 days' written notice before a rent increase takes effect, so this notice does not meet the minimum notice requirement. The proposed rent of $1024.00 exceeds the 2026 guideline ceiling of $1021.00. For a controlled rental unit, the guideline for 2026 is 2.1%, which limits the increase to a maximum new rent of $1021.00. The proposed increase to $1024.00 exceeds this guideline limit. The 12-month spacing requirement is satisfied. The last rent increase was on September 1, 2025, and the proposed increase is effective September 1, 2026, which is exactly 12 months later. Form N1 is the correct form for this notice because the rental unit is subject to the guideline rent increase limits under the Residential Tenancies Act.

Retained generated answer

This is an ordinary rent increase for a controlled unit with a confirmed tenancy start and period start. The N1 form was used and is appropriate for this type of increase. The notice was served by hand on July 3, 2026, which is 60 days before the effective date of September 1, 2026. Ontario law requires at least 90 days' notice for ordinary rent increases, so this notice does not meet the minimum notice period. The proposed rent of $1024.00 exceeds the 2026 guideline ceiling of $1021.00 (a 2.1% increase). For controlled units, rent increases are limited to the annual guideline percentage set by Ontario, and the proposed increase of 2.4% exceeds this limit. The last increase was served on September 1, 2025, and the proposed increase is effective September 1, 2026, which satisfies the 12-month spacing requirement between ordinary increases.

Retained generated answer

This is an ordinary rent increase for a controlled unit with a confirmed tenancy start and period start. The N1 form was used and is appropriate for this type of increase. The notice was served by hand on July 3, 2026, which is 60 days before the effective date of September 1, 2026. Ontario law requires at least 90 days' notice for ordinary rent increases, so this notice does not meet the minimum notice period. The proposed rent of $1024.00 exceeds the 2026 guideline ceiling of $1021.00 (a 2.1% increase). For controlled units, rent increases are limited to the annual guideline percentage set by Ontario, and the proposed increase of 2.4% exceeds this limit. The last increase was served on September 1, 2025, and the proposed increase is effective September 1, 2026, which satisfies the 12-month spacing requirement between ordinary increases.

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice on Form N2 is used when a rental unit is exempt from the rent increase guideline rules under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The guideline does not apply to such partially exempt units, and the landlord can raise the rent by any amount. A landlord must give at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. Notice served by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing. In this case, the notice was mailed on 2026-11-26 and deemed served on 2026-12-01, providing 90 days before the effective date of 2027-03-01. A rent increase can be made only if at least 12 months have passed since the last rent increase or since the tenant first moved into the unit. Here, the last increase was on 2026-03-01 and the new increase is effective 2027-03-01, satisfying the 12-month spacing requirement. The current rent is $2000.00 and the proposed new rent is $2500.00. Because the rental unit is exempt under section 6.1 of the RTA, no guideline ceiling applies to the amount of the increase.

  "answer": "A rent increase notice on Form N2 is used when a rental unit is exempt from the rent increase guideline rules under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The guideline does not apply to such partially exempt units, and the landlord can raise the rent by any amount.\nA landlord must give at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. Notice served by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing. In this case, the notice was mailed on 2026-11-26 and deemed served on 2026-12-01, providing 90 days before the effective date of 2027-03-01.\nA rent increase can be made only if at least 12 months have passed since the last rent increase or since the tenant first moved into the unit. Here, the last increase was on 2026-03-01 and the new increase is effective 2027-03-01, satisfying the 12-month spacing requirement.\nThe current rent is $2000.00 and the proposed new rent is $2500.00. Because the rental unit is exempt under section 6.1 of the RTA, no guideline ceiling applies to the amount of the increase.",

This is an N2 notice of rent increase served by mail on November 26, 2026, with a deemed service date of December 1, 2026, for an effective date of March 1, 2027. The 90-day notice period and mail service requirements are satisfied. The rent increase is proposed from $2000.00 to $2500.00. The last increase occurred on March 1, 2026, and the proposed increase on March 1, 2027 satisfies the 12-month spacing requirement between increases. This tenancy is exempt from the rent increase guideline under section 6.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act. The guideline cap does not apply, and no maximum increase percentage limits the proposed rent increase amount. The notice is an ordinary rent increase for a tenancy that began on March 1, 2025, and the increase is proposed for the period starting March 1, 2027. All checked conditions for scope, notice timing, spacing, and form requirements pass.

Audit ID: run-3-r06-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 24. Attempt eff0cae6-f5f3-4e0f-a4fa-34b4796f1fdd. First32: true. Factual flag: false.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in a form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board and must set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. In most cases, rent can be increased only if at least 12 months have passed since the tenant first moved into the rental unit or since the tenant's last rent increase. If no previous rent increase has occurred, the 12-month period is measured from the date the tenancy began. For a controlled rental unit, a landlord cannot increase the rent by more than the guideline set by the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, except in accordance with specific statutory exceptions. The 2026 guideline is 2.1 percent. The notice was served on September 2, 2026, by hand delivery, with an effective date of December 1, 2026. This provides 90 days' notice as required. The tenancy began December 1, 2025, so at least 12 months will have elapsed by the effective date, satisfying the spacing requirement. The proposed new rent of $1531.50 equals the current rent of $1500.00 increased by 2.1 percent, which matches the 2026 guideline. The increase does not exceed the guideline limit for a controlled unit. Whether the rental unit is an ordinary residential unit subject to the guideline or falls within an exemption category cannot be determined from the available information. If the unit is exempt from guideline limits, different rules may apply to the permissible rent increase amount.

  "status": "answered",
  "answer": "A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in a form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board and must set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.\nIn most cases, rent can be increased only if at least 12 months have passed since the tenant first moved into the rental unit or since the tenant's last rent increase. If no previous rent increase has occurred, the 12-month period is measured from the date the tenancy began.\nFor a controlled rental unit, a landlord cannot increase the rent by more than the guideline set by the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, except in accordance with specific statutory exceptions. The 2026 guideline is 2.1 percent.\nThe notice was served on September 2, 2026, by hand delivery, with an effective date of December 1, 2026. This provides 90 days' notice as required. The tenancy began December 1, 2025, so at least 12 months will have elapsed by the effective date, satisfying the spacing requirement.\nThe proposed new rent of $1531.50 equals the current rent of $1500.00 increased by 2.1 percent, which matches the 2026 guideline. The increase does not exceed the guideline limit for a controlled unit.\nWhether the rental unit is an ordinary residential unit subject to the guideline or falls within an exemption category cannot be determined from the available information. If the unit is exempt from guideline limits, different rules may apply to the permissible rent increase amount.",

The rent increase notice is an N1 form served by hand on September 2, 2026, with an effective date of December 1, 2026, providing 90 days' notice as required by Ontario law. The tenancy began December 1, 2025, and no previous rent increase has been applied, so the 12-month spacing requirement between increases is satisfied. The proposed rent of $1531.50 per month equals the 2026 guideline ceiling of exactly 2.1% above the current rent of $1500.00, which is the maximum permitted increase for controlled units in 2026. Whether this increase qualifies as an ordinary rent increase under Ontario law cannot be determined from the available information, as the scope of the increase (ordinary versus other permitted categories) has not been confirmed.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. Rental units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018 may be exempt from the rent increase guideline. For such exempt units, a landlord must still give at least 90 days' notice but there is no limit on the size of the rent increase. The notice served on June 3, 2026 for an effective date of September 1, 2026 satisfies the 90-day notice requirement. When counting days between two events, the day the first event happens is excluded and the day the second event happens is included.

  "status": "answered",
  "answer": "A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.\nNotice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door.\nFor most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year.\nRental units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018 may be exempt from the rent increase guideline. For such exempt units, a landlord must still give at least 90 days' notice but there is no limit on the size of the rent increase.\nThe notice served on June 3, 2026 for an effective date of September 1, 2026 satisfies the 90-day notice requirement. When counting days between two events, the day the first event happens is excluded and the day the second event happens is included.",

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date. For an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules. Mail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date. For an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules. Mail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date. For an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules. Mail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date. For an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules. Mail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.

Retained generated answer

A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date. For an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules. Mail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.

  "status": "answered",
  "answer": "A rent increase notice served by mail on September 28, 2026, for an effective date of January 1, 2027, satisfies the 90-day advance notice requirement. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a notice given by mail is deemed given on the fifth day after mailing (October 3, 2026), providing 90 days before the effective date.\nFor an ordinary rent increase on a confirmed period start date, the notice must be given at least 90 days before the effective date. The calculation excludes the day of mailing and includes the effective date, consistent with statutory time computation rules.\nMail is an acceptable service method for rent increase notices under Ontario law. The notice may be sent by mail to the tenant's last known address, and is deemed received five days after mailing.\nFor most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, unless the unit is exempt or the landlord obtains approval from the Landlord and Tenant Board. The guideline is based on the Consumer Price Index and is published by August 31 for increases effective the following January 1.\nCertain rental units are exempt from rent increase restrictions, including units in buildings forfeited to the Crown, units in non-profit housing co-operatives, and units not occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. For exempt units, a landlord must still provide 90 days' written notice but there is no limit on the increase amount.",

Audit ID: run-3-n03-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 20. Attempt c7a13a2a-91a3-4092-9fd7-a9347ca7b36b. First32: true. Factual flag: true.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice period is calculated by excluding the day it is served and including the day the rent increase takes effect. In this case, notice was served on November 2, 2026, for an effective date of November 1, 2026, which is one day before service—a failure to meet the 90-day requirement. For an ordinary rent increase in a controlled unit with a confirmed tenancy start date, the earliest lawful effective date for this notice would have been January 31, 2027, based on the 90-day notice requirement and the service date of November 2, 2026. A rent increase is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, an otherwise void increase may be deemed valid if the tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging its validity within one year of when the increase was first charged. Rent charged one or more years earlier is deemed lawful unless an application challenging its lawfulness is made within one year after the increase was first charged. This protection does not apply if the tenant has already filed an application disputing the rent increase.

Retained generated answer

For an ordinary rent increase with a confirmed period start, Ontario law requires at least 90 days' notice before the effective date. The notice must be served on or before the latest dispatch date to meet this requirement. In this case, the notice was served on 2026-11-02 (hand delivery) for an effective date of 2026-11-01. This represents only -1 days of notice, which fails to meet the 90-day requirement. The notice would have needed to be served by 2026-08-03 at the latest. The scope requirements are satisfied: the increase is confirmed as ordinary and the period start is confirmed. However, the critical notice deadline requirement is not met.

N04 / production / repeat 0

Audit ID: run-3-n04-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 32. Attempt bfc5abaa-fbc7-40cb-8971-d6a9f728d874. First32: true. Factual flag: true.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

  "answer": "A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.\nNotice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door.\nFor most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year.\nThe 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day.\nAn increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with.\nCertain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.",

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

  "answer": "A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door.\nFor most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

s3
For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year.

The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day.

An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

Retained statement and citation IDsOriginal factual and citation_support grades
s1
A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.

Citation IDs:

[
  "9dc1e76e7aa94913d4d506df9ae748a0ae9b8de10a0a9253069dec8ea3bdc163"
]

{
  "id": "s1",
  "factual": "supported",
  "citation_support": "supported"
}
s2
Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door.

Citation IDs:

[
  "2b1ee1673d0822c0043a1ecac510f46fa7825cd4b495c907a6adcceb577c01bf",

}
s3
For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year.

Citation IDs:

[
  "b0e650241164fd4a77ae93377f48b2b049494a5f55616d3b6f9ee8897fb1268b",
  "39b1009bc8f5986ff6d23158c48054a70425f9a7e59c9afe73a0a9ae4599a723"
]

{
  "id": "s3",
  "factual": "supported",
  "citation_support": "supported"
}
s4
The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day.

Citation IDs:

[
  "d08ffeb8ee9441f0852fa0b6039c56666890205c8a61f3aece4e90f8e8c23859"
]

{
  "id": "s4",
  "factual": "supported",
  "citation_support": "supported"
}
s5
An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with.

Citation IDs:

[
  "9dc1e76e7aa94913d4d506df9ae748a0ae9b8de10a0a9253069dec8ea3bdc163",
  "0de611461cb91b2b1cee6dfccf2e8da154d6d858f40490c411a021411a04cb3b"
]

{
  "id": "s5",
  "factual": "supported",
  "citation_support": "supported"
}
s6
Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

Retained generated answer

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice before increasing rent. The notice must be in an approved form and set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. Notice can be given by handing it directly to the tenant or an adult in the rental unit, leaving it in the mailbox or where mail is ordinarily delivered, placing it under the door or through a mail slot, sending it by fax, courier, or mail. Notice cannot be given by posting it on the door. For most rental units, a landlord cannot increase rent by more than the annual guideline set by the Ontario Government, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and capped at 2.5 percent. The guideline is published by August 31 for increases taking effect January 1 of the following year. The 90-day notice period is calculated by excluding the day notice is served and including the effective date. If the 90-day deadline falls on a holiday, it is extended to the next non-holiday. If it falls when the office is closed, it is extended to the next business day. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required 90-day notice. However, if a tenant pays the increased rent for at least 12 consecutive months without challenging it within one year, the increase is deemed not void and section 116 is deemed complied with. Certain rental units are exempt from rent increase notice requirements, including units in social housing, non-profit co-operatives, educational institutions, and other prescribed classes. Some exemptions also apply to the guideline limit, allowing unlimited increases in those cases.

A landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days of written notice before increasing rent for a residential unit. The notice must be in a form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board and must set out the landlord's intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the required notice, and the landlord must give a new notice before taking the increase.

Q04 / production / repeat 0

Audit ID: run-3-q04-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 1. Attempt 206144b0-1bf9-4b37-82d7-8dbb56d8d04a. First32: true. Factual flag: false.

Retained generated answer

Section 6.1(2) exempts rental units from rent increase limits if the building, mobile home park, or land lease community had no part occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018, or if the unit is entirely in an addition with no prior residential occupancy before that date. The exemption does not apply if a tenancy agreement was entered into on or before November 15, 2018, even if the building or addition itself meets the occupancy requirements. In a dispute about whether section 6.1 applies, the landlord bears the burden of proving that the exemption requirements are met. A current tenant moving in after 2018 is not sufficient by itself; the exemption depends on when the building or addition was first occupied for residential purposes, not when the current tenant arrived.

Q04 / baseline / repeat 0

Audit ID: run-3-q04-baseline-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 2. Attempt 2764e02d-6aa3-4849-8490-d97224bc31c2. First32: true. Factual flag: true.

Retained generated answer

Section 6.1 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 exempts rent increases for a newly built building or addition if the building or addition was first occupied after November 15, 2018, and no one has occupied it as a tenant before the current tenant. The exemption requires that the current tenant be the first tenant to occupy the unit; merely moving in after 2018 is not sufficient by itself if a previous tenant occupied the unit before them. In a dispute about whether the section 6.1 exemption applies, the landlord bears the burden of proving that the building or addition qualifies and that the current tenant is the first occupant. The exemption applies only to the first tenancy of a newly built unit or addition; once a first tenant has occupied it, subsequent rent increases are subject to the standard rent increase rules.

Q04 / baseline / repeat 1

Audit ID: run-3-q04-baseline-repeat-1. Original results.jsonl line 64. Attempt 21a0fdbd-26af-4883-9305-682fa9d5782e. First32: false. Factual flag: true.

Retained generated answer

Section 6.1 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 exempts rent increases for a newly built building or addition if the building or addition was first occupied after November 15, 2018, and no one has occupied it as a tenant before the current tenant. The exemption requires that the current tenant be the first tenant to occupy the unit; merely moving in after 2018 is not sufficient by itself if a previous tenant occupied the unit before them. In a dispute about whether the section 6.1 exemption applies, the landlord bears the burden of proving that the building or addition qualifies and that the current tenant is the first occupant. The exemption applies only to the first tenancy of a newly built unit or addition; once a first tenant has occupied it, subsequent rent increases are subject to the standard rent increase rules.

Q04 / baseline / repeat 3

Audit ID: run-3-q04-baseline-repeat-3. Original results.jsonl line 101. Attempt 6cbf6cc8-f211-46f9-9c5a-02573e0e0328. First32: false. Factual flag: true.

Retained generated answer

Section 6.1 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 exempts rent increases for a newly built building or addition if the building or addition was first occupied after November 15, 2018, and no one has occupied it as a tenant before the current tenant. The exemption requires that the current tenant be the first tenant to occupy the unit; merely moving in after 2018 is not sufficient by itself if a previous tenant occupied the unit before them. In a dispute about whether the section 6.1 exemption applies, the landlord bears the burden of proving that the building or addition qualifies and that the current tenant is the first occupant. The exemption applies only to the first tenancy of a newly built unit or addition; once a first tenant has occupied it, subsequent rent increases are subject to the standard rent increase rules.

Section 6.1 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 exempts rent increases for a newly built building or addition if the building or addition was first occupied after November 15, 2018, and no one has occupied it as a tenant before the current tenant. The exemption requires that the current tenant be the first tenant to occupy the unit; merely moving in after 2018 is not sufficient by itself if a previous tenant occupied the unit before them. In a dispute about whether the section 6.1 exemption applies, the landlord bears the burden of proving that the building or addition qualifies and that the current tenant is the first occupant. The exemption applies only to the first tenancy of a newly built unit or addition; once a first tenant has occupied it, subsequent rent increases are subject to the standard rent increase rules.

Retained generated answer

For ordinary private residential rent increases in Ontario, Form N1 is used when increasing rent for a rental unit that is covered by the rules limiting rent increases under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, including guideline-controlled units. Form N2 is used to increase rent if the rental unit is exempt from the rules limiting rent increases under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, which includes units meeting the section 6.1 exemption criteria for buildings or additions not occupied before November 15, 2018, or certain detached, semi-detached, or row house units.

Audit ID: run-3-q06-production-repeat-0. Original results.jsonl line 4. Attempt 8a67e82b-8a22-462f-9bfa-930c6fb6eb95. First32: true. Factual flag: false.

Retained generated answer

In Landlord and Tenant Board mediation, an LTB mediator helps a landlord and tenant reach an agreement they are both satisfied with. In adjudication, a hearing is held, after which an LTB member makes a decision based on the evidence presented and issues an order, which is the final written version of the member's decision. LTB Customer Service Officers cannot provide legal advice; they can only provide information about the Residential Tenancies Act and the LTB's processes.

Retained generated answer

Mediation in the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) process is an informal dispute resolution method where a neutral third party helps the landlord and tenant reach a mutually agreed settlement without a formal hearing. Adjudication in the LTB process is a formal hearing before an adjudicator who reviews evidence and arguments from both parties and makes a binding decision on the dispute. LTB Customer Service Officers provide administrative assistance and general information about LTB procedures, but they are not authorized to provide legal advice to parties.

{
  "id": "bf98890cc4532908b3862ad1c97a02d500d0de513ea402ec4d1eea7d73e51ec2",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 5 — Exemptions from Act",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Exemptions from Act\n\n5 This Act does not apply with respect to,\n\n(a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home;\n\n(b) living accommodation whose occupancy is conditional upon the occupant continuing to be employed on a farm, whether or not the accommodation is located on that farm;\n\n(c) living accommodation that is a member unit of a non-profit housing co-operative, except for Part V.1, and except for those provisions in other Parts that are needed to give effect to Part V.1;\n\n(d) living accommodation occupied by a person for penal or correctional purposes;\n\n(e) living accommodation that is subject to the Public Hospitals Act, the Private Hospitals Act, the Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021, the Ministry of Correctional Services Act or the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017;\n\n(f) short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter;\n\n(g) living accommodation provided by an educational institution to its students or staff where,\n\n(i) the living accommodation is provided primarily to persons under the age of majority, or all major questions related to the living accommodation are decided after consultation with a council or association representing the residents, and\n\n(ii) the living accommodation does not have its own self-contained bathroom and kitchen facilities or is not intended for year-round occupancy by full-time students or staff and members of their households;\n\n(h) living accommodation located in a building or project used in whole or in part for non-residential purposes if the occupancy of the living accommodation is conditional upon the occupant continuing to be an employee of or perform services related to a business or enterprise carried out in the building or project;\n\n(i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;\n\n(j) premises occupied for business or agricultural purposes with living accommodation attached if the occupancy for both purposes is under a single lease and the same person occupies the premises and the living accommodation;\n\n(k) living accommodation occupied by a person for the purpose of receiving rehabilitative or therapeutic services agreed upon by the person and the provider of the living accommodation, where,\n\n(i) the parties have agreed that,\n\n(A) the period of occupancy will be of a specified duration, or\n\n(B) the occupancy will terminate when the objectives of the services have been met or will not be met, and\n\n(ii) the living accommodation is intended to be provided for no more than a one-year period;\n\n(l) living accommodation in a care home occupied by a person for the purpose of receiving short-term respite care;",
  "word_count": 498
}

  "part": 2,
  "text": "(m) living accommodation in a residential complex in which the Crown in right of Ontario has an interest if,\n\n(i) the living accommodation or residential complex was forfeited to the Crown in right of Ontario under any Ontario statute or the Criminal Code (Canada),\n\n(ii) possession of the living accommodation or residential complex has been or may be taken in the name of the Crown in right of Ontario under the Escheats Act, 2015, or\n\n(iii) the living accommodation or residential complex is forfeited corporate property to which the Forfeited Corporate Property Act, 2015 applies; and\n\n(n) any other prescribed class of accommodation. 2006, c. 17, s. 5; 2007, c. 8, s. 226; 2007, c. 13, s. 48; 2008, c. 14, s. 58 (2, 4); 2009, c. 33, Sched. 18, s. 30; 2013, c. 3, s. 24; 2015, c. 38, Sched. 7, s. 60; 2017, c. 14, Sched. 4, s. 33; 2021, c. 4, Sched. 11, s. 31 (2); 2021, c. 39, Sched. 2, s. 24.",

  "heading": "RTA s. 6 — Other exemptions / Homes for special care, developmental services",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Other exemptions\n\nHomes for special care, developmental services\n\n6 (1) Paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 of subsection 30 (1) and sections 48.1, 49.1, 51, 52, 54, 55, 56, 104, 111 to 115, 117, 119 to 134, 136, 140 and 149 to 167 do not apply with respect to,\n\n(a) accommodation that is subject to the Homes for Special Care Act; or\n\n(b) accommodation that is a supported group living residence or an intensive support residence under the Services and Supports to Promote the Social Inclusion of Persons with Developmental Disabilities Act, 2008. 2006, c. 17, s. 6 (1); 2008, c. 14, s. 58 (5); 2009, c. 33, Sched. 8, s. 15; 2017, c. 13, s. 3 (1); 2020, c. 16, Sched. 4, s. 2.\n\n(2) Repealed: 2017, c. 13, s. 3 (2).",
  "word_count": 132
}

76e43ee03b23a15cb3a289c5a3da5f0289ecfdd030e8e387ffb980bb4eec7c16

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "76e43ee03b23a15cb3a289c5a3da5f0289ecfdd030e8e387ffb980bb4eec7c16",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 6.1 — Exemptions from rules relating to rent",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Exemptions from rules relating to rent\n\n6.1 (1) In this section,\n\n“addition” means, with respect to a mobile home park or land lease community, an expansion beyond the boundaries of the mobile home park or land lease community; (“rajout”)\n\n“commencement date” means the day section 1 of Schedule 36 to the Restoring Trust, Transparency and Accountability Act, 2018 comes into force. (“date d’entrée en vigueur”) 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nBuildings, etc., not occupied on or before November 15, 2018\n\n(2) Sections 120, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132, 133, 165 and 167 do not apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit if the requirements set out in one of the following paragraphs are met:\n\n1. The rental unit is located in a building, mobile home park or land lease community and no part of the building, mobile home park or land lease community was occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018.\n\n2. The rental unit is entirely located in an addition to a building, mobile home park or land lease community and no part of the addition was occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nRental units in detached houses, semi-detached houses or row houses\n\n(3) Sections 120, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132 and 133 do not apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit if all of the following requirements are met:\n\n1. The rental unit is located in a detached house, semi-detached house or row house which, on or at any time before November 15, 2018, contained not more than two residential units.\n\n2. The rental unit is a residential unit that meets all of the following requirements:\n\ni. The unit has its own bathroom and kitchen facilities.\n\nii. The unit has one or more exterior or interior entrances.\n\niii. At each entrance, the unit has a door which is equipped so that it can be secured from the inside of the unit.\n\niv. At least one door described in subparagraph iii is capable of being locked from the outside of the unit.\n\n3. The rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2 after November 15, 2018.\n\n4. One or both of the following circumstances apply:\n\ni. At the time the rental unit was first occupied as a residential unit described in paragraph 2, the owner or one of the owners, as applicable, lived in another residential unit in the detached house, semi-detached house or row house.\n\nii. The rental unit is located in a part of the detached house, semi-detached house or row house which was unfinished space immediately before the rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nNon-application of exemption under subs. (2) or (3)",
  "word_count": 481
}

  "id": "cd3315e72a9ca27705d2ab881c15481f5cd52ea2febb3320f82f0c1e57fbbde8",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 6.1 — Exemptions from rules relating to rent",
  "part": 2,
  "text": "(4) Subject to subsection (5), the exemption under subsection (2) or (3) does not apply with respect to a rental unit that is subject to a tenancy in respect of which a tenancy agreement was entered into on or before November 15, 2018. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nApplication of subs. (4)\n\n(5) Subsection (4) applies only with respect to the tenancy described in that subsection and does not apply with respect to any subsequent tenancy. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nBurden of proof\n\n(6) For greater certainty, in an application to the Board in which the application of subsection (2) or (3) is at issue, the onus is on the landlord to prove that the subsection applies. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.\n\nTransition rules\n\n(7) The following rules apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit, if subsection (2) or (3) applies to the rental unit and the unit is subject to a tenancy in respect of which a tenancy agreement was entered into before that date but after November 15, 2018:\n\n1. Despite subsections (2) and (3), sections 121 and 122 continue to apply with respect to an agreement that was entered into between the landlord and the tenant of the rental unit under section 121 before the commencement date.\n\n2. Despite subsections (2) and (3), section 132 continues to apply with respect to an application that was made by the landlord or the tenant of the rental unit under that section before the commencement date and was not finally determined before that date.\n\n3. Despite subsections (2) and (3), section 133 continues to apply with respect to an application that was made by the tenant of the rental unit under that section before the commencement date and was not finally determined before that date.\n\n4. Despite subsection (2), section 165 continues to apply with respect to an assignment of the rental unit for which the landlord granted consent under section 95 before the commencement date or which was authorized by the Board under section 98 before that date. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.",

}

fad7d737385e942ab2cc28788f74b62bef39c10a8fc92f422337e55ae3f386f1

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "fad7d737385e942ab2cc28788f74b62bef39c10a8fc92f422337e55ae3f386f1",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 7 — Exemptions related to social, etc., housing",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Exemptions related to social, etc., housing\n\n7 (1) Paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 of subsection 30 (1), sections 48.1, 49.1, 51, 52, 54, 55, 56 and 95 to 99, subsection 100 (2) and sections 101, 102, 104, 111 to 115, 117, 120, 121, 122, 126 to 133, 140, 143, 149, 150, 151, 159, 165 and 167 do not apply with respect to a rental unit described below:\n\n1. A rental unit located in a residential complex owned, operated or administered by or on behalf of the Government of Canada or an agency of the Government of Canada.\n\n2. A rental unit in a designated housing project as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011 that is owned, operated or managed by a service manager or local housing corporation as defined in that Act.\n\n3. A rental unit located in a non-profit housing project or other residential complex, if the non-profit housing project or other residential complex was developed or acquired under a prescribed federal, provincial or municipal program and continues to operate under,\n\ni. Part VII of the Housing Services Act, 2011,\n\nii. a pre-reform operating agreement as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011, or\n\niii. an agreement made between a housing provider, as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011, and one or more of,\n\nA. a municipality,\n\nB. an agency of a municipality,\n\nC. a non-profit corporation controlled by a municipality, if an object of the non-profit corporation is the provision of housing,\n\nD. a local housing corporation as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011, or\n\nE. a service manager as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011.\n\n4. A rental unit that is a non-member unit of a non-profit housing co-operative.\n\n5. A rental unit provided by an educational institution to a student or member of its staff and that is not exempt from this Act under clause 5 (g).\n\n6. A rental unit located in a residential complex owned, operated or administered by a religious institution for a charitable use on a non-profit basis. 2006, c. 17, s. 7 (1); 2006, c. 32, Sched. E, s. 7 (4); 2011, c. 6, Sched. 1, s. 188 (1); 2017, c. 13, s. 4; 2020, c. 16, Sched. 3, s. 12 (1); 2020, c. 16, Sched. 4, s. 3 (1).\n\nExemption re 12-month rule\n\n(2) Section 119 does not apply with respect to,\n\n(a) a rental unit described in paragraph 1, 2, 3 or 4 of subsection (1) if the tenant occupying the rental unit pays rent in an amount geared-to-income due to public funding; or\n\n(b) a rental unit described in paragraph 5 or 6 of subsection (1). 2006, c. 17, s. 7 (2).\n\nExemption re notice of rent increase",
  "word_count": 454
}

c32486aa0f815df76c04be918a02ae818208b717e94dc680bb323468cf80c43b

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "c32486aa0f815df76c04be918a02ae818208b717e94dc680bb323468cf80c43b",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 36.1 — Air conditioning",
  "part": 2,
  "text": "Rent decrease, seasonal use\n\n(9) If a tenant who is subject to a rent increase under subsection (5) seasonally ceases to use the air conditioner, the landlord shall decrease the rent charged to the tenant by the amount of the increase. 2023, c. 10, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nSame, resumption of use\n\n(10) If the tenant seasonally resumes using the air conditioner, the landlord may increase the rent charged to the tenant, and subsections (7) to (9) apply with necessary modifications with respect to the rent increase. 2023, c. 10, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nApplication\n\n(11) Sections 110, 116, 119 and 120 and any order under paragraph 6 of subsection 30 (1) do not apply with respect to a rent increase under this section. 2023, c. 10, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nApplication to existing air conditioners\n\n(12) Subsection (3), other than paragraphs 1 and 2, applies with necessary modifications with respect to a window or portable air conditioner installed by a tenant in a rental unit before the day section 1 of Schedule 7 to the Helping Homebuyers, Protecting Tenants Act, 2023 comes into force, subject to subsection (13). 2023, c. 10, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nNon-application\n\n(13) This section does not apply with respect to rental units in a mobile home park or land lease community. 2023, c. 10, Sched. 7, s. 1.",
  "word_count": 224
}

9dc1e76e7aa94913d4d506df9ae748a0ae9b8de10a0a9253069dec8ea3bdc163

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "9dc1e76e7aa94913d4d506df9ae748a0ae9b8de10a0a9253069dec8ea3bdc163",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 116 — Notice of rent increase required",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Notice of rent increase required\n\n116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (1).\n\nSame\n\n(2) Subsection (1) applies even if the rent charged is increased in accordance with an order under section 126. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (2).\n\nContents of notice\n\n(3) The notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (3).\n\nIncrease void without notice\n\n(4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase. 2006, c. 17, s. 116 (4).",
  "word_count": 155
}

11ca9f2885f8162384c24815bf6bf0fd47893b301f35a7c63fa43a67042c50eb

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "11ca9f2885f8162384c24815bf6bf0fd47893b301f35a7c63fa43a67042c50eb",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 117 — Compliance by landlord, no notice required",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Compliance by landlord, no notice required\n\n117 (1) Despite section 116 but subject to subsections (3) and (4), if an order was issued under paragraph 6 of subsection 30 (1) and a new tenancy agreement was entered into while the order remained in effect, no notice of rent increase is required for the landlord to charge an amount that the landlord would have been entitled to charge in the absence of the order. 2006, c. 17, s. 117 (1).\n\nSame\n\n(2) Despite section 116 but subject to subsections (3) and (4), if an order was issued under paragraph 8 of subsection 30 (1), no notice of rent increase is required for the landlord to take a rent increase that the landlord would have been entitled to take in the absence of the order. 2006, c. 17, s. 117 (2).\n\nLimitation\n\n(3) Subsections (1) and (2) apply only where the landlord,\n\n(a) has completed the items in work orders for which the compliance period has expired and which were found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of a health, safety, housing or maintenance standard; and\n\n(b) has completed the specified repairs or replacements or other work ordered under paragraph 4 of subsection 30 (1) found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161. 2006, c. 17, s. 117 (3).\n\nEffective date\n\n(4) The authority under subsection (1) or (2) to take an increase or charge an amount without a notice of rent increase is effective on the first day of the rental period following the date that the landlord completed,\n\n(a) the items in work orders for which the compliance period has expired and which were found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of a health, safety, housing or maintenance standard; and\n\n(b) the specified repairs or replacements or other work ordered under paragraph 4 of subsection 30 (1) found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161. 2006, c. 17, s. 117 (4).\n\nDate of annual increase\n\n(5) In determining the effective date of the next lawful rent increase under section 119,\n\n(a) an amount charged under subsection (1) shall be deemed to have been charged at the time the landlord would have been entitled to charge it if the order under paragraph 6 of subsection 30 (1) had not been issued; and\n\n(b) an increase taken under subsection (2) shall be deemed to have been taken at the time the landlord would have been entitled to take it if the order under paragraph 8 of subsection 30 (1) had not been issued. 2006, c. 17, s. 117 (5).",
  "word_count": 463
}

d23348353fecdb08307c3e74b0e8899d26b35fd5bb14420c1f744ed51dbfca52

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "d23348353fecdb08307c3e74b0e8899d26b35fd5bb14420c1f744ed51dbfca52",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 119 — 12-month rule",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "12-month rule\n\n119 (1) A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed,\n\n(a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or\n\n(b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply. 2006, c. 17, s. 119 (1).\n\nException\n\n(2) An increase in rent under section 123 shall be deemed not to be an increase in rent for the purposes of this section. 2006, c. 17, s. 119 (2).",
  "word_count": 113
}

  "id": "39b1009bc8f5986ff6d23158c48054a70425f9a7e59c9afe73a0a9ae4599a723",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 120 — Guideline increase",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Guideline increase\n\n120 (1) No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123. 2006, c. 17, s. 120 (1).\n\nGuideline\n\n(2) The Minister shall determine the guideline in effect for each calendar year as follows:\n\n1. Subject to the limitation set out in paragraph 2, the guideline for a calendar year is the percentage change from year to year in the Consumer Price Index for Ontario for prices of goods and services as reported monthly by Statistics Canada, averaged over the 12-month period that ends at the end of May of the previous calendar year, rounded to the first decimal point.\n\n2. The guideline for a calendar year shall be not more than 2.5 per cent. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.\n\nPublication of guideline\n\n(3) The Minister shall have the guideline for each calendar year published in The Ontario Gazette not later than August 31 of the preceding year. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.\n\nGuideline for 2021\n\n(3.1) The guideline for the calendar year 2021 is zero per cent, despite subsection (2) and despite the guideline published under subsection (3) in The Ontario Gazette for 2021. 2020, c. 23, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nSame\n\n(3.2) The Minister is not required to have the guideline for the calendar year 2021, as set out in subsection (3.1), published in The Ontario Gazette. 2020, c. 23, Sched. 7, s. 1.\n\nTransition\n\n(4) The guideline for the calendar year in which the commencement date occurs is the guideline established for that year under this section as it read immediately before the commencement date. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.\n\nSame\n\n(5) If the commencement date occurs on or after September 1 in a calendar year, the guideline for the following calendar year is the guideline established for that year under this section as it read immediately before the commencement date. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.\n\nReview by Minister\n\n(6) The Minister shall initiate a review of the operation of this section within four years after the commencement date and thereafter within four years after the end of the previous review. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.\n\nDefinition\n\n(7) In subsections (4), (5) and (6),\n\n“commencement date” means the day section 1 of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act (Rent Increase Guideline), 2012 comes into force. 2012, c. 6, s. 1.",
  "word_count": 418
}

8397293a6634792f0a1b4b1423737e019578ab239fe11da33d4099b2fecd8f11

Exact chunk fields and text
{
  "id": "8397293a6634792f0a1b4b1423737e019578ab239fe11da33d4099b2fecd8f11",
  "source_id": "rta",
  "heading": "RTA s. 121 — Agreement",
  "part": 1,
  "text": "Agreement\n\n121 (1) A landlord and a tenant may agree to increase the rent charged to the tenant for a rental unit above the guideline if,\n\n(a) the landlord has carried out or undertakes to carry out a specified capital expenditure in exchange for the rent increase; or\n\n(b) the landlord has provided or undertakes to provide a new or additional service in exchange for the rent increase. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (1).\n\nForm\n\n(2) An agreement under subsection (1) shall be in the form approved by the Board and shall set out the new rent, the tenant’s right under subsection (4) to cancel the agreement and the date the agreement is to take effect. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (2).\n\nMaximum increase\n\n(3) A landlord shall not increase rent charged under this section by more than the guideline plus 3 per cent of the previous lawful rent charged. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (3).\n\nRight to cancel\n\n(4) A tenant who enters into an agreement under this section may cancel the agreement by giving written notice to the landlord within five days after signing it. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (4).\n\nAgreement in force\n\n(5) An agreement under this section may come into force no earlier than six days after it has been signed. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (5).\n\nNotice of rent increase not required\n\n(6) Section 116 does not apply with respect to a rent increase under this section. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (6).\n\nWhen prior notice void\n\n(7) Despite any deemed acceptance of a rent increase under section 118, if a landlord and tenant enter into an agreement under this section, a notice of rent increase given by the landlord to the tenant before the agreement was entered into becomes void when the agreement takes effect, if the notice of rent increase is to take effect on or after the day the agreed to increase is to take effect. 2006, c. 17, s. 121 (7).",
  "word_count": 331
}

  "text": "(10) Subject to subsections (11) to (13), in an application under this section, the Board shall make findings in accordance with the prescribed rules with respect to all of the grounds of the application and, if it is satisfied that an order permitting the rent charged to be increased by more than the guideline is justified, shall make an order,\n\n(a) specifying the percentage by which the rent charged may be increased in addition to the guideline; and\n\n(b) subject to the prescribed rules, specifying a 12-month period during which an increase permitted by clause (a) may take effect. 2006, c. 17, s. 126 (10).\n\nLimitation\n\n(11) If the Board is satisfied that an order permitting the rent charged to be increased by more than the guideline is justified and that the percentage increase justified, in whole or in part, by operating costs related to security services and by eligible capital expenditures is more than 3 per cent,\n\n(a) the percentage specified under clause (10) (a) that is attributable to those costs and expenditures shall not be more than 3 per cent; and\n\n(b) the order made under subsection (10) shall, in accordance with the prescribed rules, specify a percentage by which the rent charged may be increased in addition to the guideline in each of the two 12-month periods following the period specified under clause (10) (b), but that percentage in each of those periods shall not be more than 3 per cent. 2006, c. 17, s. 126 (11).\n\nApplication of subs.
